turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's curiosity is piqued by the inconsistencies in Mr. Worthing's account, and she asks him to clarify the matter of his mother's identity.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that his mother, who passed away when he was young, was a lady of the name of Emily Fairfax, but he had not seen her in person and had only heard stories about her.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell insisted that a man of respectable birth and breeding would have known his mother's maiden name, and she asked Mr. Worthing to provide a satisfactory explanation for his ignorance on this point.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen tapped on the carriage window, demanding to be let down to join the conversation.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Mr. Worthing was a bachelor when he knew his mother, and he had not paid much attention to family details, he explained.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell turned to Jack and Gwendolen, her voice stern and inquiring, as she asked, 'Mr. Worthing, it is imperative that you provide a more satisfactory explanation for your ignorance regarding your mother's maiden name.'

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she would not be ignored and that she would join the conversation immediately, and she began to get out of the carriage.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's voice took on a stern tone as she demanded a clear and honest explanation from Mr. Worthing regarding his mother's maiden name, her eyes narrowing in warning that any further evasion would not be tolerated.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: He explained that he had been led to believe that his mother's name was Smith, and he had not thought to question it.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told her mother that she would not stand idly by while her fiancé was being interrogated, and that she would like to hear a satisfactory answer to the question herself.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing that his explanation was unsatisfactory and that he would need to provide further evidence of his legitimacy, her voice dripping with disapproval.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen insisted that her mother was being unjustly harsh on Jack and that he was perfectly respectable

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen to refrain from interrupting and allow her to continue questioning Mr. Worthing, her voice firm and authoritative.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told her mother that she was beginning to think that this line of questioning was nothing but a thinly veiled attempt to discourage her engagement to Mr. Worthing

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell's eyes narrowed as she scrutinized Jack, her voice dripping with skepticism as she told Gwendolen that she was still not entirely convinced by his account of his parentage, and that she required further proof of his legitimacy before she could consider his suitability as a husband for her daughter.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen asked her mother if she was truly so concerned about the Worthing family's legitimacy or if she was simply trying to drive a wedge between her and Jack.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen to refrain from making such impertinent remarks and to allow her to focus on the matter at hand, which was the suitability of Mr. Worthing as a husband for her daughter

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he understood the need for verification of his parentage and assured Lady Bracknell that he would be happy to provide any necessary documentation.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell turned to Gwendolen and instructed her to remind Mr. Worthing that, in the event of their marriage, he would be expected to provide for her in a manner befitting her station and family connections.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen told her mother that she would not be lectured on the duties of marriage, and that she was perfectly capable of managing her own affairs.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Gwendolen and Mr. Worthing to pardon her, as they were not engaged to anyone. She explained that when they did become engaged, she or Mr. Worthing's father, if his health permitted, would inform them of the fact. An engagement should come as a surprise to a young girl, and it was hardly a matter she could arrange for herself. While she was making inquiries, Gwendolen would wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen called out to Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to wait for her in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen replied to Lady Bracknell that she would wait for her.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Mr. Worthing to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stood tall, his eyes locked on Lady Bracknell, and said that he preferred to remain standing, rather than take a seat.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell informed Mr. Worthing that he was not on her list of eligible young men, although she had the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. However, she was willing to enter his name if his answers were satisfactory. She asked him if he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing admitted to Lady Bracknell that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing smoked. She believed that a man should have an occupation. There were too many idle men in London. She asked Mr. Worthing how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that twenty-nine was a good age to get married. She believed that a man who wanted to get married should know either everything or nothing. She asked Mr. Worthing which category he fell into.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell was pleased to hear that Mr. Worthing knew nothing. She believed that ignorance was a delicate and exotic fruit that should not be tampered with. She stated that education was unsound and produced no effect in England. If it did, it would be a danger to the upper classes. She asked Mr. Worthing about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing if his income came from land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing replied to Lady Bracknell that his income came from investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell thought that Mr. Worthing's income was satisfactory. She stated that land was no longer a profit or pleasure, but rather a means of gaining position and losing it. She asked Mr. Worthing about his country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land, but he did not depend on it for his income. In fact, the poachers were the only ones who made anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing how many bedrooms his country house had. She also asked if he had a town house, as a girl like Gwendolen could not be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing who Lady Bloxham was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack observed that Lady Bracknell went out very little, and that she was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Mr. Worthing what number his house in Belgrave Square was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Mr. Worthing told Lady Bracknell that his house was number 149.
